newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. thrown off key U.N. financial committee. [CORRECTED 10:46 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. thrown off key U.N. financial committee. [CORRECTED 10:46 GMT]

text.p: The United States was voted off a key U.N. financial committee for the first time on Friday, a reflection of countries' anger at Washington's $1.4 billion debt to the world body, U.S. officials said.

Instead France and New Zealand were given spots on the prestigious 16-member Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (ACABQ), the first legislative step in reviewing the U.N.'s $1.3 billion annual budget.
Diplomats said it was the first time the United States, which is supposed to pay 25 percent of the U.N. budget, was not given a seat on the panel of financial experts.

The vote by secret ballot was in the General Assembly's administrative and budgetary committee, which includes all 185 countries with U.N. membership. It makes the final decision on the budget, which the Assembly then usually rubber stamps.

France received 117 votes followed by New Zealand with 116 and 103 votes for the United States. French envoys said they did not campaign against Washington, assuming it would automatically get one of the two (Corrects from three) vacant seats for which it was eligible.

"We congratulate New Zealand and France and we regret deeply the narrow defeat of the United States," said a U.S. official, adding that the vote was particularly distressing because of the high qualifications of the U.S. candidate, Melinda Kimble.
"The lack of our participation will inevitably diminish the committee," she said.
Kimble had been chosen carefully this year after U.S. allies had questioned the competence of some previous U.S. appointments, diplomats said.

The U.S. official noted that budgetary decisions would be made by the full committee and that U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright would continue to battle for fiscal restraint and a continuation of the United Nations' no-growth budget.
Asked why the U.S. lost, the official said, "Three things: money, money and money. The resentment of U.S. arrears to the United Nations was clearly the decisive factor."
Other American envoys admitted that the lack of a seat of the committee would make it more difficult than ever to get funds from the Republican-dominated Congress.

Many Republicans have been severely critical of the United Nations, regardless of reforms it has initiated. U.S. envoys had hoped budget cuts, which have been ongoing for two years, as well as a new secretary-general, would convince Congress to abide by U.S. international commitments.

The United States owes the world body about $1.4 billion for dues and peacekeeping, more than half of the U.N.'s entire debt. Washington has also vowed to veto Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in his bid to serve another five-year term, which may have been another factor in the vote.

Japanese and Western Europeans, who pay the bulk of U.N. costs, have been openly criticial of U.S. demands for reforms when it failed to pay its debts. In addition, U.S. influence has waned because of severe cuts in international non-military aid programmes around the world.
